The parent cartridge of the .22/250 was the .250/3000 savage which saw light of day in 1915 for the Savage model 99 lever action rifle. The .250 Savage was the first commercial cartridge to breech the 3000 fps barrier. Well for such a hot cartridge it wasn't long before the wildcatters took notice. Among those early wildcatters were Grosvenor Wotkyns, J.E Gebby, and J. Bushnell Smith. The .22/250 reached is final configuration in 1937. From 1937 to 1963 if you wanted a .22/250 you had to have your favorite gunsmith build you a custom rifle. My .22/250 was built by the Gunsmith Birck Munson, of Twin Falls Idaho in 1954. The base receiver is a M1903 Spring filed. The Barrel is a Douglas Segment-ally rifled premium barrel. The telescopic sight is 1950 Weaver K10 (That was the best there was back then). The wood is American White Ash.

Two years later (1965) Remington offered their Model 700 and their model XB40 Match rifle chambered for the .22/250. At the same time Remington began producing the .22/250 ammunition naming it the .22/250 Remington. The rest is history as they say. Pictures man. Your posts are pretty good. I liked the "how to fit a match barrel and bushing for 1911" post, but I need a visual aid. On another note. I have a 4.25" 1911 with a bull barrel. Would it be possible to fit a 5" threaded barrel and conventional barrel bushing to it?

A heavier barrel (called a bull barrel after Freeman R. Bull) a weapons smith for Springfield armory and a noted long range marksman of the day (1887) built a heavier barrel for the Model 1873 Trapdoor Springfield to control muzzle motion. That style of barrel has been used on match weapons ever since.

I can see no reason why you would have a so called bull barrel on a M1911. I know that Brownells sells an STI barrel that they call a bull barrel (but isn't) to eliminate the barrel bushing from a M1911. I read that they claim that they get better lock up and accuracy (but I have my doubts). The locking of the barrel to the slide occurs at the rear of the barrel just forward of the chamber. The barrel has to tilt down slightly (controlled by the barrel link) to allow the locking lugs to disengage from the slide. This tilting action will impact the accuracy of a unbushed weapon as by necessity there has to be a loose fit at the front of the slide to allow tilting. A properly fitted bushed barrel allows the barrel to be pull straight back until the bearing surface at the barrel muzzle is no longer in contact with the bushing. The relieved barrel (smaller diameter) now allows the barrel to tilt to unlock from the slide. It is the precise fitting of the barrel to the bushing to the slide that Makes the M1911 style weapon so accurate over a wide range of conditions. If you would check you will find that the bushed M1911 has won almost all large bore championships for the last 50 years.

I don't know where you are going to get a 5 inch barrel for a M1911. Most long slide conversions of the M1911 use a 6 inch barrel and a slide that is 1.75 inches longer than the standard M1911 slide. Now as for threading. That means you are going to have to cut off a 6 inch barrel and re-crown it which is a rather tricky thing to do. Then when you make your thread cuts into the metal of the barrel you are going to weaken it somewhat and also create areas for stress fractures to occur. (the sharp valley of the threads)

I suspect that you are going to got through all this so you can thread a silencer on it. Have your computed the additional weight of the silencer and what it is going to effect the recoiling of the weapon. You may think that you are going to weaken the recoil spring to make up for the additional weight of the barrel and silencer but remember the barrel only recoils about a quarter of an inch. so now you have a weak spring on a normal weigh slide and you might get short stroking or failure to feed and failure of the weapon to lock into battery, because you do not have sufficient spring pressure to force the heavy barrel with its silencer up onto the locking ramp.
